The socialist housing plan for New York City

As rental prices in New York City soar, tenant activists are demanding that the government stop landlords from increasing the rent on regulated apartments. In the end, these lucky tenants would get relatively cheap apartments while everyone else ends up worse off. Reason speaks with housing advocates, landlords, experts, and working-class New Yorkers struggling to find a place to call home, and gets a first-hand look at the city’s housing crisis. As mayoral candidate Zohran Mamdani gets closer to winning his election—and freezing rents for nearly 2 million New Yorkers—many fear that the situation will only get worse.

Rent Got SO High... Millions of People Are Living in Hotels Now

More Americans are living in hotels—not because they want to, but because traditional housing has become unaffordable or inaccessible. With rent prices skyrocketing, cost of living rising, credit checks tightening, deposits increasing, and utilities adding up, extended-stay hotels are becoming a last-resort solution for people trying to survive the current housing crisis.

This video breaks down why hotel living is becoming more common, how inflation and rising housing costs are pushing people out of apartments and homes, and the real financial math behind these decisions. From $1,200 monthly hotel stays with no credit checks to families living long-term in extended stays, this is a look at how bad the housing situation has really become—and why this trend should worry everyone.

If you care about personal finance, housing affordability, cost-of-living realities, and how everyday people are adapting to an economy that’s squeezing them, this breakdown puts the situation into perspective

People Are Replacing Rent With Hotels… And It’s Actually Working

With rent prices rising across the country, some people are trying something unexpected — living in hotels instead of renting apartments. No lease, no utilities, and sometimes even weekly discounts that can make the price surprisingly competitive with traditional housing.

In this video we’re taking a closer look at the growing trend of people choosing hotel living, how they’re making it work, what it actually costs, and whether it’s really as smart as it sounds. We’ll also talk about the legal gray areas around long-term hotel stays, residency rules, and whether this trend could eventually affect hotel pricing if it keeps growing.

Is living in a hotel a clever workaround for expensive rent… or a temporary solution with hidden downsides?

content:
Tourism's hidden price: Mallorca's housing crisis | DW Documentary

The Spanish island of Mallorca is a popular holiday destination. But short term rentals and rising property prices are forcing more and more locals out of their neighborhoods.

Millions of tourists come to the island every year. But many Mallorcans can no longer afford the rents here. 60-year-old Begoña is a parking inspector. She and her son Hector, who works as a waiter, live in a caravan in Palma, Mallorca’s capital. Their combined income of 2,500 euros isn’t enough to afford an apartment. A 22-year-old medical student, Christofer lives in a stuffy basement room in Palma and pays 600 euros a month. The conditions are catastrophic: the sewage pumps are defective and it smells awful, and the power is often out. These are just 2 stories from the growing problem of Mallorca’s housing shortage.

What is your monthly rent? Comment below!

What is your monthly rent? ₹8,000 in a small town or ₹35,000 in a metro? Now ask yourself the harder question. How much of your salary is left after paying it? Across India’s big cities like Mumbai, Bengaluru, Delhi NCR and Hyderabad, rent has quietly become the single largest monthly expense for young professionals and middle class families.

On paper, India is one of the fastest growing major economies in the world. GDP numbers look strong. Infrastructure is expanding. Startups are booming. But at the ground level, many households feel financially squeezed. When rent rises faster than salaries, savings shrink. Risk taking reduces. Career changes feel dangerous. Even basic life decisions like marriage, moving cities or starting a business get delayed because housing eats up stability.

More than 2,000 condos sitting empty in Metro Vancouver amid housing crisis

More than 2,000 new condos in Metro Vancouver are sitting unsold and empty despite an ongoing housing crisis and steep rental prices, according to a recent report.

The report by real estate agency rennie found the number is predicted to rise to nearly 3,500 condos by the end of 2025. In addition, pre-sales are so low that it is forcing some developers to rethink current projects.

As Alissa Thibault reports, at least one analyst say it's a combination of economic uncertainty and low affordability.

We explain how homes stopped being homes and turned into investment tools, why prices keep rising even when nobody’s buying, how Wall Street firms like Blackstone and Invitation Homes now own thousands of houses, and why landlords today are often hedge funds instead of humans.

You’ll also learn about land hoarding, zombie houses, Airbnbs replacing locals, and how government “solutions” often make the problem worse. Finally, we explore if renting is becoming the new normal and what could actually fix this broken system.

Using simple language, real-life examples, and clear visuals, we reveal why the dream of home ownership keeps slipping away for millions around the world.
